title: CS Quest 6.1 · Tech that changed the world
name: Tech that changed the world
summary: Students vote on eight technology dilemmas in Would You Rather (live) and defend a side with a tradeoff: who is helped, who is hurt, which job changes. The Timeline Walk hangs twelve inventions on a rope, each with a job it created and a job it changed. No game and no live warm-up today.
iCan: compare the tradeoffs of a technology for everyday life
say which jobs a technology creates and which jobs it changes
materials: Invention timeline cards printable (12 cards, one per pair)
a rope or long string across the room, with clothespins or tape
paper strips for the plus and minus notes
the Would You Rather prompt sheet (printed with the plan)
doNow: Write one thing your grandparents did without a computer that you do with one. Whose job did that change?
plan: Timeline Walk: invention cards on the rope
Would You Rather (live): Tech choices, 8 dilemmas

do: Draw a T-chart on the board for the self-checkout: left, everyday life (faster lines, no waiting); right, careers (fewer cashier jobs, new technician jobs). Fill it with the class in one minute.
Hang the telephone card and the video call card at the two ends of the rope and ask who used each this week.
say: Advances in technology are neither all good nor all bad. The way people use them has tradeoffs: a benefit over here, a cost over there.
Automation means a machine does a task people used to do. It changes jobs more than it removes them: the cashier's work shrinks and the technician's work grows.
ask: Driverless cars could cut some accidents. What is the cost side of that T-chart?
explore.afterAsk: Collect three answers (drivers' jobs, hacking, who is to blame in a crash). Say that today every vote comes with the same question: who is helped, who is hurt, what job changes.
explore.bigIdea: Every technology is a tradeoff: it helps someone's day and changes someone's job.

play.defend: every other reveal: one student for A, one for B, thirty seconds each; the scaffold for this band is: who is helped, who is hurt, what job changes
play.room: start the room from the plan page with your class picked so the run lands in class history; an open room is fine when students are not signed in

steps: Each pair gets one invention card. Pairs hang it on the rope where they think it belongs in time, oldest on the left.
Pairs write two strips for their card: a plus strip (a job this invention creates) and a minus strip (a job it changes or shrinks), and hang them under the card.
Walk the rope together for two minutes: read the strips out loud, and for two cards ask the privacy question too: what does this one know about you?

lookFors: a tradeoff with only one side: ask for the job on the other side of the T-chart
privacy answers that stop at it is creepy: push for what data is collected and who can see it
play.misconception: Students think automation simply deletes jobs; the point of the lesson is that it changes jobs, removing some tasks and creating others, and the tradeoff lands differently on different people.
earlyFinishers: add a third strip to a neighbor's card: who decides whether this technology gets used?
put an invention nobody brought on the rope with its two job strips

discuss: Which invention on the rope would you un-invent for a week? Who would be better off, and who would be worse off?
Pick the closest vote. Which job does each side change, and who was not asked?
showMe: Show the class split for the dilemma with the closest vote on the projector; one student per side gives the benefit and the cost in one sentence each.

exit.sentencePrompt: Pick one technology from today. Name a benefit for everyday life and a cost for someone's job or privacy.
exit.frame: ___ changed how people ___. The tradeoff is ___.

rubric.line: Tech changes: compares a tradeoff for everyday life and for jobs
levels: Names a technology and one effect
Names a benefit and a cost of the same technology
Compares both sides for everyday life and for a career or privacy, and says who is affected

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: the T-chart stays on the board with the headings everyday life and careers
defenders may read the printed prompt first and answer only its question
the host reads each dilemma out loud before the timer starts
stretch: influenced by culture: why do emoji exist, and who decides which ones get made?
write the third column: who decides whether this technology gets used, and who is not asked

unpluggedTwin.title: Corners vote
materials: the printed dilemma sheet (the 8 dilemmas of the live run)
a sign for corner A and a sign for corner B
the invention timeline cards, the rope and the paper strips
steps: Read a dilemma out loud. Students walk to corner A or corner B. Count hands out loud and write the split on the board.
After every other dilemma, one student from each corner has thirty seconds to defend their side with the scaffold: who is helped, who is hurt, what job changes.
Finish with the Timeline Walk as in the plan: the rope, the cards, a job created and a job changed for each.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: write one thing your grandparents did without a computer that you do with one, and whose job that changed.

Run the Corners vote with the printed dilemma sheet (walk to corner A or B, count hands, two defenders every other round), then the Timeline Walk: each pair hangs its invention card on the rope with a strip for a job it created and a strip for a job it changed. No projector and no login needed.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Which invention on the rope would you un-invent for a week? Who would be better off, and who would be worse off?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut; shorten the walk along the rope, not the strips

add: host 10 dilemmas instead of 8 (the plan page's block-day starter) with defenders on every reveal
the full Timeline Walk with the third column: who decides, who is not asked
10 minutes of the Unit 6 pre-test: the unit opener and review items on the projector

notes: No live warm-up today on purpose: the vote is the warm-up. The warm-up of 6.2 opens with this unit's opener item.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: invention.
Start the room from the plan page with your class picked so the run lands in class history; an open room is fine when students are not signed in, and the step is then completed by participation.
Driverless cars, self-checkout and map apps are the exit items: use them in the T-chart and the walk.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Write one thing your grandparents did without a computer that you do with one. Whose job did that change?

Big idea: Every technology is a tradeoff: it helps someone's day and changes someone's job.

Timeline Walk: hang your invention card on the rope where it belongs in time. Under it, hang a plus strip (a job it created) and a minus strip (a job it changed).

We will talk about:
- Which invention would you un-invent for a week? Who would be better off, and who would be worse off?
- Pick the closest vote. Which job does each side change?

steps.title: Would You Rather (live)
steps.body: Eight dilemmas about technology. Vote, then look at how the class split. When your teacher picks you, defend your side for thirty seconds: who is helped, who is hurt, what job changes.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about technology tradeoffs.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
Pick one technology from today. Name a benefit for everyday life and a cost for someone's job or privacy.
Frame: ___ changed how people ___. The tradeoff is ___.
